chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
title: Studying with Jaroslav Cimera in Chicago
summary: After joining Hines he took lessons from the Polish teacher, prompted by Billy Franklin and Louis Taylor, and became his most apt student.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: In fact I never really took a trombone lesson from a good trombone teacher until I got with Earl Hines. I never did really take an interest in really getting to the foundation, the basics of it. And then once I started it was hard to stop because it was like a new world to me, something I really enjoyed doing, you know.

I'll never forget what made me do it was I was playing with two trombone players who had studied with Earl Hines. And it was Billy Franklin and Louis Taylor. And Louis Taylor had studied with a Polish gentleman in Chicago. His name was Jerry -- Gerislav Shimera (PHONETIC) And he lived way out in Oak Park in Chicago. So, it was a long subway ride. I lived on the South Side and that was a long -- about a 45 minute ride out on -- all the way out to Jerry's home.

And when I first went out there he asked me to play a B flat scale for him. So, I think it was so horrible, what I played was so bad until -- he asked me where did I work. So, I told him. He said you get paid for playing. So, I told him yeah. He shook his head, you know. He wondered how, you know, because -- well, I could play jazz. I really had no -- I didn't know nothing about intonation. I didn't know anything about it.
And these two guys did. So, they said, look, if you're going to play with us you got to work on your tone, and you got to do this and that. And, you know, but I never

worried about that. I had a hard enough time playing the notes, you know. So after working in Tommy Miles' band we never did -- intonation wasn't one of our strong points. Let's put it that way, you know.

But these guys were more professional, you know, who were playing in that band. And there were some good guys in that band. So, I worked hard. I went out to this teacher, and he showed me what to do. And I'll never forget. He was charging $2.00 a lesson back there then. That was a lot of money, you know, back there then because when I first went with Earl, I think I was making about oh, $40-45.00 a week, you know. And that was a lot of money, $2.00.

Anyway, so -- I stayed -- I went to this man and I got carried away. I was intrigued. I didn't know that all these things went on with the trombone. So -- and I'd go from week -- every week I'd go. I worked hard at it. And he was a funny man. He told me, he says if you don't study, don't come back next week. I don't -- I'm not looking for students, he said, because I can get all the students I want.

At the same time I was going to him some top trombone players in some of the top bands were studying with him. Tommy Peterson was studying with him at that time. So was Eddie Cosby. Eddie Cosby's name is Eddie Cosboski, but he changed it to Eddie Cosby. But we all were studying with him at that time, and I didn't know they were going to turn out to
be top trombone players. And they didn't know it was going to happen to me.

But he was a very meticulous man. He didn't care who you were. If you were serious about it he would help you. Because after he found out I was serious he told me, look, if you don't have any money come out anyway and take your lesson. Because -- and he paid me a high compliment later on in later years. He said I was the most apt student that he ever had. You know, it really made me feel good because he had some really fantastic trombone players that studied with him. I felt it was a great honor for him to have mentioned that about me.
